beta_new: Alternate between stemming, laybacking and plain face climbing as you work up the corner on the flake to the shared anchor.

On the first pitch, climb the face to a bolt over a little roof, then work rightward past a second bolt and a crack angling left. Edge and smear across the sloping slab above, clipping further bolts, up to a delicate crux under a triangular niche. Belay there if rope drag builds, or keep going.

Scramble around rightward to a belay perch, then lieback and undercling the left-slanting flake system under the overhang. Work up a sharp arete on edges, pass a tight corner facing left, and finish through a headwall to the anchors set at the lip.
Pumpy moves lead up the leaning wall past three bolts; stretching far right and then returning left keeps the difficulty down. Above, an easy slab runs to anchors beside a hanging block.
Follow That Crack for the first 20 feet, then shift left and crank up the overhanging black arete to the high anchors.
Pitch one aids the vertical crack, which leans out slightly and bulges near the top, up toward the belay spot; most of it is fixed. Pitch two ends along a slim crack.

moves.from: Pins and nuts, in modest numbers, make up the rack.

value.text: A modest number of pins and nuts.

beta_new:
Begin up Technosurfing: a corner facing left leads to the broken band of rock, and from there you traverse over to chains on a ledge. Clip in, then haul the rope off the lower bolts so it doesn't drag higher up.

Pull over a bulge into an open corner, work leftward then back right to the foot of the huge roof near the clifftop, and swing across exposed jugs onto a pumped-out lip and the dangling anchors.

Climb the short corner (a medium cam protects it) and continue on buckets through the leaning wall into a broken zone. Above, edge your way up a gentler open book, sitting on the roof's left, to reach the anchors.
Use good edges to head up and right inside the overhanging corner, with fun laybacks around a flake leading to the rim. The anchors are off to the left.
Face climb past the bolts, getting across a small roof partway, and continue to the anchor.

Find the obviously overhanging crack system. Work leftward along a slanting seam of lumpy rock, then wrestle over a big flake to a straddling rest on top of it. A tricky corner facing right, with two bolts, leads to a hands-free head-jam rest.

Above that, pinch holds, laybacks and kneebars carry you up the pumpy flake system to a ledge from which to clip the chain anchor.
Follow great edges up the outer side of the pillar, and carry a mid-sized cam to protect the crack beyond the second bolt.
Face climb for about twenty feet past three bolts, then head leftward into a crack lodged behind the flake. Edge rightward beneath the slanting corner to the lip anchors.

moves.from: A small tech Friend is useful.

beta_new: Begin at the ramp's lower-left end and climb easy rock until the initial bolt. Powerful moves on overhanging rock follow, then you pull onto a rest. Work leftward on jugs and finally back right to the chains at the lip.

An awkward, shallow corner facing left takes you to a first rest, then you head up and left across a pumpy, cool-looking bulge to another good rest. Technical, easier rock finishes at the anchor on the horizontal break.
Work a bolt-protected bouldery sequence along the outer left margin of the cave.

Start slightly left where it is easier, or ascend directly on solid holds for roughly fifty feet, arriving at a two-bolt stance. The second pitch is a long traverse rightward; use whatever fixed gear is there and look after your second.

Find the thin corner that faces right, down and right from where Thin Air begins. Traverse up and right over shelves and rubbly granite until you stand left of the bottom of the corner, climb its right face until you can step left, then continue up its outer arete past a pair of short headwalls to the chains.

A delicate bouldery opening leads about twelve feet to an eyebolt under a short corner facing right. Rock over onto the ledge, then climb the fractured whitish band, passing through an inverted V up toward a roof.

Undercling under the roof, clip the bolt past its lip, pull over, trend up a leaning slab, then finish leftward on an arete to anchors at a stance.
Leave the ledge beside the prominent arete and reach the first bolt, then transfer to the arete's other face using layback and crimp holds past five more bolts.
Pull over a series of bulges on good holds, ending at anchors above a tight corner.

Start down and right of Thin Air, where a corner angles right. Take the easy flake for a few moves rightward, then trend leftward by a fixed piton toward a long, slim roof.

The crux is edging over that roof. Move up the face toward a fixed pin, mantle onto a bolt above, and angle left by a few more pegs to the belay stance.

The first pitch is the access ledge shared with The Eliminate. On pitch two, start from the tree ledge immediately left of that route, ascend a flake and aid-climb five bolts across a featureless wall toward a belay ledge. The third pitch follows a lengthy upright corner at left.
Around the bend left of Wedged, a right-facing corner contains a chimney narrow enough to squeeze. Squirm your way to the pinnacle's summit.

moves.from: then face climb to descend from it

beta_new: Haul on buckets across bulges, clipping three bolts, until you reach a solid rest. Above that, edge your way up a steep, slabby wall whose rock has vertical strata.

The hard part comes immediately, a bouldery sequence to a low ceiling. Then angle off leftward by a bolt to the stance. Parties can lower from there, or tackle the big overhang higher up by working out to the right.
The original way up this spire follows the north-facing front side to the summit.
The slab is gentle enough that you can set up a belay almost anywhere. The continuous crack takes gear the full length, so stop wherever suits the party.
Get up the right-facing dihedral on the left of its famous neighbor to the ledge, where the hardest move is.

moves.from: From there you can rappel off or continue on a separate easier route to the summit.

beta_new: From the ledge, pull a roof at a corner, then traverse a long way right along horizontal cracks; a medium cam helps there. Then continue upward to the finish, and look after the follower on the traverse with good placements.

On the second pitch go up into the corner that faces left, and trend rightward onto a face with a tree plus a rappel station with bolts, a popular belay. To go on, angle left beyond a small overhang, then back right beyond another to a comfortable belay ledge.

Sacajawea Peak: from the head of Thorp Creek, climb steep fell fields and talus to the ridge and follow it to the summit, the high point of the range, on pale marble and limestone. Sacajawea to the Matterhorn: the crest south carries a handful of gendarmes; stay on the spine for Class 3 moves with moderate exposure, or drop onto the west side in scree to get around them. Expect to pick a line and backtrack at times. The Matterhorn: a broad white limestone summit, easy once you reach it. Back north onto the Hurwal Divide: return toward Sacajawea and turn east along the dog-legged divide, mostly on the right-hand (south/east) side of the crest to avoid exposure, over miles of crumbling shale, talus and scree with goat paths giving occasional relief, to the Hurwal Divide high point. Hurwal Divide to Chief Joseph Mountain: descend about two miles to a saddle, then follow the Chief Joseph ridge north over several intermediate points to the dark basalt summit cap of Chief Joseph Mountain.

The route follows a steep, loose rib splitting a pair of big drainages. Keep to the rib's crest instead of dropping into the gullies on either side. Expect sections of exposure with big loose blocks, and test every hold. The rib tops out on the west (northwest) summit. From there, traverse the crest to the slightly higher east summit, then continue along the ridge crest before descending the rubbly slopes toward Crater Lake.

moves.from: Walk the East Eagle Trail up the valley for about 1.5 mi, then leave it and head right into the steep basin on Krag Peak's west side.
From the lake, pick up the Little Kettle Creek Trail and follow its many switchbacks back down to the East Eagle Trailhead.

beta_new: South Sister (10,358'): from the Devils Lake Trailhead, climb the South Sister climbers' trail through forest and onto the open plateau, then continue north up the South Ridge on steep scree, skirting the Lewis Glacier's moraine lake on its west side, to the crater rim and around to the summit - a Class 2 walk-up on loose volcanic rock. Leave the summit down the Northwest Ridge (Class 2, snow early and scree late; the Eugene Glacier snowfield lies along its flank) and drop north toward the saddle with Middle Sister above Camp Lake. Middle Sister (10,047'): climb the South Ridge, mostly big talus (Class 2), to the summit, then descend the North Ridge (Class 2-3; it can hold steep snow or ice early in the season) and follow the upper edge of the Collier Glacier to the saddle between Prouty Point and North Sister. North Sister (10,085'): scramble loose slopes onto the South Ridge and follow climbers' paths that alternate between west-side ledges and the east side at gaps. Below the summit pinnacle, cross the Terrible Traverse - a steep, exposed snowfield with a nasty runout in early and mid-summer, an easy Class 3 scree crossing once melted out - then turn up into the Bowling Alley, a steep, loose gully between the pinnacle's horns. Its headwall is easy but loose Class 4; above it, Class 2-3 leads to the summit block.

moves.from: Reverse the pinnacle and ridge to the Prouty Point saddle to start the exit.

beta_new: Begin at the foot of the big dihedral, follow the green-stained streak into the crack, then finish up the face overhead to reach the belay bolts.

First pitch: climb the face to a notch, mount it, shift left and then angle rightward, clipping a pair of bolts, to a comfortable treed ledge.

Second pitch: ascend rightward along a big flake, traverse over its top toward a little tree, then follow the dark streak directly to the summit.
Head directly up to the bolt beneath the arch, enter the arch from its left side, and surmount the bulge via its crack; two further bolts lead to the top.

moves.from: bolt beneath the arch ... two further bolts lead to the top

beta_new:
First pitch: angle leftward up to a tree set into the overlap, mantel it and clip a pair of bolts, then join the long right-rising crack-and-ledge line and stop at a belay beside another tree under the Boston flake.

Second pitch: climb the flake, step left onto the black streak, and follow that streak to the belay bolts; it is exposed and offers little protection.

First pitch: follow solid holds up a series of corners onto a ramp that slants rightward, and stop beside Fatman Flake, under a steeper headwall, to belay.

Second pitch: go up the flake, veer leftward onto a ledge, then keep climbing easy rock where no gear is available, or move left to belay at the summit.

moves.from: A modest set of nuts and cams is enough.

beta_new: Ascend the centre of the hourglass-shaped flake toward the shallow arch (small gear suits the arch crack), then edge up the thinner face above, clip a bolt, and finish straight onto a ledge for belaying.
